questions.prompt: Which of the following is the most appropriate use of AI on an underwriting file?
choices: Asking the model whether an applicant with a 1.15 DSCR and a recent bankruptcy should be approved
Asking the model to summarize the capital structure and list visible risks, with no recommendation
Asking the model to predict the probability of default given the deposit history
Asking the model to draft your committee recommendation paragraph in your voice
questions.explanation: Summarizing structure and listing visible risks is synthesis — the kind of work AI is reliably good at when constrained to restatement. Asking for an approval call, a default prediction, or a recommendation paragraph are all credit decisions the model has no basis to make and that put your judgment downstream of a system that should be downstream of yours.

questions.prompt: You ask AI to summarize a 40-page applicant file. The output reads as a clean, well-organized one-page picture. It includes a debt service coverage ratio of 1.32 that you do not recall seeing in the source documents. What is the right response?
choices: Use the figure — the model has integrated information across the file that you may have missed
Cross-check the figure against the source documents before any of it goes near a memo
Trust the figure if the rest of the summary appears accurate, since accuracy tends to cluster
Re-prompt the model and use whichever DSCR appears more often across re-runs
questions.explanation: AI will produce plausible-looking numbers that do not exist in the source. Trusting a figure because the surrounding summary looks clean is exactly the pattern that puts a fabricated DSCR in front of committee. Verification against source documents — every figure, every time — is non-negotiable. Re-prompting to look for consistency does not help; the model can confabulate consistently.

questions.prompt: Two underwriters discuss the synthesize-vs-decide rule. Which framing is most aligned with how this path expects you to use AI?
choices: 'AI should never touch a credit file because anything it produces is unreliable'
'AI is a junior analyst whose drafts I review and whose recommendations I weight alongside my own'
'AI restates and reformats the file; the call is mine, and I never ask it whether to approve'
'AI gives me a starting point on the recommendation that I then refine based on my judgment'
questions.explanation: The first option is too restrictive — AI is legitimately useful for synthesis. The second and fourth options both let the model's framing influence the credit call, which is the exact drift this lesson warns against; even 'starting point' or 'weighted alongside' lets the model shape the recommendation. Only the third option keeps the synthesize-vs-decide line clean.
